title: Motorcyclist in 20s taken to London hospital after ‘serious’ crash with bin lorry
author: Millie Bowles
content:
UK regional news website of the year
A motorcyclist has been airlifted to a London hospital after a serious crash with a bin lorry.
The A20 was shut in Sellindge, near Ashford, between Bulls Lane and Woodlees Close, this morning but has now reopened.
It followed a collision involving a bin lorry and a motorbike just before 10am.
The air ambulance, along with police and paramedics, were at the scene.
The motorcyclist - a man in his 20s - was was taken to Kings College Hospital for treatment to multiple injuries to his face and leg.
Police have described the crash as serious, and a spokesperson added: “Officers and paramedics attended and the motorcyclist, a man in his 20s, was taken to a London hospital for treatment to multiple injuries.
“His next of kin is aware.
“The road was temporarily closed while the incident was responded to and has since reopened.”
At the time of the crash, traffic information site Inrix reported queues building in both directions on the route.
summary: A motorcyclist in his 20s was airlifted to a London hospital following a serious collision with a bin lorry in Sellindge. The crash occurred just before 10am, prompting emergency services including the air ambulance, police, and paramedics to respond. The A20 was temporarily closed, causing traffic queues, but has since reopened.
key_points: A motorcyclist in his 20s sustained multiple injuries to his face and leg.
The crash involved a motorbike and a bin lorry just before 10am.
The victim was airlifted to King's College Hospital in London.
The A20 in Sellindge was temporarily closed during the response and has since reopened.

title: 'Calm space' installed at busy west London Tube station
author: Aurelia Foster
content:
![A structure with a pitched roof, paintings of greenery inside, a seat and a sign reading 'calm space'](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/2391/live/e6df3e70-a87b-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.jpg)
The space at Ealing Broadway station provides a place to pause and "reset", TfL says
- Published
A new "calm space" is being trialled at a west London Tube and railway station, aimed at helping passengers who find travelling overwhelming.
The space at Ealing Broadway station provides a welcoming, low-stimulation environment where customers can take time out to pause and rest, Transport for London (TfL) says.
It has an acoustic shelter designed to reduce surrounding noise, a comfortable seat, and is decorated with calming images of nature and plants.
The idea is being trialled as part of a TfL strategy to make travelling on the network more inclusive. The calm space at Ealing Broadway is to be followed by a second space in the London Transport Museum in Covent Garden this autumn.
The shelters have been designed with level access and with room for mobility aids, pushchairs and assistance dogs, TfL said.
![A young man walks along a platform in front of a London Underground sign with the station name Ealing Broadway on.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/3a20/live/e7170430-a863-11f1-ae45-e9984fc27c77.jpg)
TfL teamed up with autism charity Austistica to create the spaces, which worked with neurodivergent people to create the calm spaces and research what benefits they could bring.
They concluded that access to a calm space while travelling could significantly help some people and give them confidence to travel independently.
Customers are being encouraged to try out the spaces during the trials and submit feedback.
Dr Amanda Roestorf, director of research at Autistica, said: "For many neurodivergent Londoners, a calm space can be the difference between avoiding the Underground and travelling with confidence.
"These spaces offer a vital safe space to pause, regulate, and continue their journey independently."
TfL said it was continuing to improve accessibility across the network, with Â£3m a year being invested over five years to improve facilities.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: Transport for London (TfL) has introduced a trial "calm space" at Ealing Broadway station to help passengers who find travelling overwhelming. Developed in partnership with the autism charity Autistica, the low-stimulation acoustic shelter features seating and nature imagery. A second space is planned for the London Transport Museum in Covent Garden this autumn.
key_points: A new calm space trial at Ealing Broadway station aims to assist passengers who find travelling overwhelming.
The shelter features an acoustic design to reduce noise, a seat, and calming nature decorations.
The initiative was developed by TfL in partnership with the autism charity Autistica.
The shelters include level access with room for mobility aids, pushchairs, and assistance dogs.
A second calm space is scheduled to open at the London Transport Museum this autumn.

title: Rain drenches commuters as London faces wettest day in months
author: Michael Howie; Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
A band of rain is sweeping London on Tuesday, forcing thousands of commuters to reach for their umbrellas before heading to work.
The wet weather moved across the capital overnight from the west, and is expected to linger into the early afternoon.
The rain intensified as morning rush hour peaked between 8am and 9am.
Many have taken to X to complain about the wet conditions during their morning commute - while some welcomes the downpour following the record-setting hot and dry summer.
Speaking on Radio 4’s Today, BBC Weather Centre forecaster Simon King described conditions as “really quite soggy”.
“We’ve had some rain overnight across England and Wales. It’s useful rain but it’s not significant rain to alleviate the drought situation for most of us.”
He said the rain will gradually work its way south-east before dry conditions return.
“The rain will be more stubborn to clear away in the far south-east,” he added.
Temperatures in London are predicted to peak at around 20C, according to the Met Office.
That's a sharp contrast with the 28C high over the capital on Sunday as heatwave conditions briefly returned to the capital.
The warm weather continued on Monday with 25C recorded in west London.
After Tuesday's washout, more settled weather is expected in London with largely dry days through to the weekend and temperature peaks of between 20C and 23C.
The outlook after that looks reasonably good for London. The Met Office's long-range forecast predicts "a trend toward some longer dry interludes between systems as we head toward mid-September", although a return of the dry, settled weather of the summer "looks unlikely".
Temperatures are expected to be "close to average overall".
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/08/8/00/IMG_1254.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/08/8/35/IMG_1257.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Looking towards the end of September and into October, the Met Office predicts "a continuation of more settled conditions", before "more changeable" weather develops.
"Temperatures will likely be a little above average overall, with relatively cool nights possible at first tending to reduce in frequency later in the period," it says.
summary: Heavy rain swept across London on Tuesday, disrupting the morning commute and marking the wettest day in months following a hot and dry summer. The wet weather is expected to clear towards the southeast by the early afternoon, giving way to more settled and dry conditions through the rest of the week. Temperatures are predicted to reach a peak of around 20C, contrasting sharply with the 28C highs recorded over the weekend.
key_points: A band of rain moved across London overnight and intensified during the morning rush hour.
BBC forecaster Simon King noted the rain is not significant enough to alleviate the ongoing drought.
Tuesday's wet weather follows a record-setting hot summer and recent weekend temperatures of up to 28C.
Met Office forecasts predict largely dry and settled weather for London through the weekend and into mid-September.

title: Star Trek branding beams onto the London Underground
author: Ian Mansfield
content:
Star Trek branding beams onto the London Underground
The London Underground has been teleported to Beta Quadrant after a Star Trek 60th anniversary advertising campaign was turbolaunched this morning.
![](https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/star-trek-60-london-underground-01.jpg)
Just two stations, and if you’re not a fan of station rebranding, rest assured this is so subtle it’s almost too easy to miss that it’s happening. A few decals at South Kensington and King’s Cross St Pancras station, and mostly adverts for Samsung televisions in a branding tie-in with Star Trek.
However, there are also tannoy announcements — and these are very Star Trek branded, with a transporter sound opening and then themed messages. One references the infamous Tribbles, and another replaces the See It, Say It, Sort It message (which is as ubiquitous as Tribbles these days, and just as annoying).
According to the Star Trek website, the branding campaign runs today and tomorrow (7th and 8th September).
There is also a Star Trek event at the Samsung store at King’s Cross, and a Star Trek themed late opening at the Science Museum on Tuesday evening.
summary: A Star Trek 60th anniversary advertising campaign has launched on the London Underground, featuring subtle station decals and themed tannoy announcements. The promotion, which is tied to Samsung televisions, runs for two days on September 7th and 8th. Additional events include a Star Trek activation at the King's Cross Samsung store and a themed late opening at the Science Museum.
key_points: A Star Trek 60th anniversary advertising campaign is running on the London Underground on September 7th and 8th.
Decals and themed tannoy announcements with transporter sounds are featured at South Kensington and King’s Cross St Pancras stations.
The branding includes a tie-in with Samsung televisions.
Related events include a Samsung store activation at King's Cross and a themed late opening at the Science Museum.

title: London Playbook PM: PLP? This is hardcore
author: Emilio Casalicchio
content:
Good afternoon. This is Emilio Casalicchio.
MONDAY CHEAT SHEET
— Andy Burnham is braced for a grilling from Labour MPs worried about losing their seats.
— John Healey urged ministers to throw legal caution to the wind in their decision-making — and was compared with Rachel Reeves.
— The government announced a big U-turn from the Keir Starmer era on local council reform due to … legal risk.
— The date for the race to replace Starmer in Holborn and St Pancras has been set.
— A Reform conference performance sparked a row between Boney M members.
**A message from Shell UK: More than 10,000 people have already engaged with our SkillsTransition programme, helping to build the UK’s energy workforce. It's one of the many ways we're investing in people, while providing secure and reliable energy that UK homes and businesses depend on every day. Find out more, and see disclaimer: shell.co.uk/about-us**
TOP OF THE NEWSLIST
PLP? THIS IS HARDCORE: Andy Burnham is gearing up for a behind-closed-doors grilling with eager Labour MPs desperate to find out whether his premiership will indeed save their political butts.
Separations: The new prime minister will face his skittish PLP on committee corridor from 6 p.m. and will need more than surviving longer than Liz Truss to convince them his administration offers a clear break with the past. Coverage of the Big Speech from John Healey this morning isn’t helping.
His ‘n’ hers: Even some Labour MPs are arguing Rachel Reeves could have made the speech her successor delivered in the Midlands this morning, which was big on tackling regulation and directing government investment — with a splash of devolution thrown in — in the hope growth might emerge from the other end.
Growth freaks: Standing in front of two massive robotic arms in a warehouse at the Manufacturing Technology Centre outside Coventry, Healey said his “defining mission as chancellor is growth,” adding that he wanted to “make Great Britain growth Britain again.”
The measures: Healey said he would make further reforms to the HMT “green book” (which decides where investment goes) aimed at backing projects with more long-term potential … urged ministers to ditch most consultations and tolerate a higher level of legal risk to speed up decision-making (new guidance here — although remember we’ve heard this stuff before, even as recently as March) … and said he would extend the list of projects exempt from judicial review.
Surprise, surprise: “John Healey sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves,” said Conservative Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith. Reform economic spokesperson Robert Jenrick chimed in that Healey was “beginning to make even Rachel Reeves seem inspiring.”
No doubt taking a wry interest in all this is … Reeves herself, who was holding meetings in PCH this afternoon as a newly minted former chancellor.
One area where Healey is not like Reeves: The new chancellor took four questions from the press after his speech and ignored the sole patient hand up in the room from the person unwilling to play the game of begging aides for a question in advance. Reeves used to take numerous questions at her press conferences, then take a few from hands up at the end to make sure the whole thing wasn’t a total stitch-up. Happier times for the press.
Taxing questions: The four broadcasters who did get questions wanted to know whether Healey might raise taxes in the upcoming budget — which he of course was never going to spell out. He did, however, note in his speech he wanted to “draw a line” under ever-rising costs for business — which sounded a bit like a promise for no Reeves-esque national insurance hikes. Lib Dem economic spokesperson Daisy Cooper said the government should indeed be “changing course” after heaping costs onto firms, and the Institute for Government published a piece in the past few minutes urging another look at the three main taxes on individuals.
Different class: The new chancellor tried to convince voters his budget will be a break from the past, arguing he’s acknowledged their desperation for the “change” promised in 2024 — which Reform continues to capitalize on despite their internal woes. “We will not deliver all this tomorrow,” Healey said. “But we’re delivering the start of it today. I recognise the urgency of the moment.”
But will that recognition actually be acted on? That’s the question MPs will be asking Burnham at the PLP tonight. Those Playbook PM spoke to said they want to hear what’s changed under his leadership and what his top priorities are — with at least one quipping that he needs to call a snap election for a fresh, reforming mandate. Backbenchers are eager to get their local areas on his radar (with many facing challenges from either Reform or the Greens) and want to know what devolution means outside the north, what he thinks about their big issues and more. MPs want regular access to ministers and a role in turning Burnham’s priorities into change in their seats — and not be informed about decisions after the fact.
Not helping on that front: Communities Secretary Angela Rayner this afternoon told the Commons she’s cancelling decisions to reform some local councils and reviewing plans to reform others — backtracking on a significant tenet of the Starmer era. Rayner said she had made the decision following legal advice — which doesn’t quite chime with the pledges about weathering higher legal risk. And Nigel Farage claimed Reform court challenges prompted the change — which doesn’t quite chime with his anger about courts blocking government decisions.
Not pleased: Labour MPs were not impressed about being told about the change of heart at the last minute. One said Burnham was “meant to have a better grip on PLP relations,” adding: “It was a nice couple of weeks of thinking maybe things could be better.” There was frustration in the Commons over the past hour or so. Expect it to become a bone of contention at the PLP meeting.
What else MPs will want to talk about: No doubt some at the PLP will take the chance to make demands about the budget. For example, almost 30, including former Shadow Chancellor Anneliese Dodds and Business Minister Gareth Thomas, wrote to Healey this afternoon urging him to introduce a Fair Banking Act to encourage more affordable loans. “Expanding access to affordable credit would help make life more affordable while also supporting growth, keeping more money in the pockets of those who need it most and helping to prevent manageable financial setbacks from spiralling into serious debt,” reads the letter, which my POLITICO colleague Noah Keate got hold of.
Other budget ideas: Former Chancellor Jeremy Hunt told the World at One he hopes “none of the major parties promise to keep the triple lock going into the next election.” He said he has been advising current Shadow Chancellor Griffith that the pensions guarantee should be ditched “over time.” If only he’d been in government and had the chance to do it himself — that might have been more effective than bottling it and hoping someone else does it.
| ![](https://www.politico.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/03/NSR08498-Shell-Politico_Playbook-BannerAd_w300xh250px-AWv1-FO.jpg) | 
DRIVETIME DEBRIEF
IT’S A DATE: Voters in Holborn and St Pancras will go to the polls on October 8, POLITICO’s Dan Bloom revealed shortly before the writ was moved in the Commons. With a closely fought battle expected between Labour and the Greens, the date matters tactically. One Green figure told our Isabel Loubser that early October means students won’t have time to register — which could pose problems for Zack Polanski.
But he has an earlier problem than that: Green candidate selection is still to take place, and the leader now faces some competition. Camden councilor Hamza Chowdhury threw down the gauntlet this morning, arguing the area doesn’t need another MP who “puts out a few leaflets, makes a few promises and disappears once the voters are counted.” Miaow. Although Isabel hears only polite words were exchanged when the pair went door-knocking last week, and Chowdury might clarify that his comments referred to Starmer — not his own boss.
Race to the doors: It’s a long time since Holborn and St Pancras has been the beneficiary of significant Labour campaign resources, but now even the foreign sec is being sent out on the doors. Deputy Labour Leader Lucy Powell insisted “Andy Burnham’s message of hope is really cutting through.” We’ll see on October 9.
THE FOREIGN SEC HAS BIGGER FISH TO GRILL: No.10 is having an official row with U.S. ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, after he said (in relation to some Ed Miliband comments about Gaza) that “Jew hate” in the British government “knows no boundaries.” A spokesperson for Andy Burnham this morning told reporters “we completely reject that assertion.”
MANDARIN MUTTERINGS: Elsewhere in Mili-world, Whitehall insiders expect him to land on his choice for top dog at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office in the coming days, my colleague Esther Webber texts in. Trump whisperer Karen Pierce and High Commissioner to India Lindy Cameron are known to be in the frame, but Esther hears Deputy National Security Adviser Barbara Woodward is also still in the running. That would mean the department will get its first female permanent secretary no matter what.
HAPPENING NOW: Home Office Minister Sarah Jones is delivering a ministerial statement in the Commons about the protests in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend. Treasury Minister Emma Reynolds (who is doing her own statement on the Healey speech afterwards) condemned the “thuggish and intimidating behavior” during the protests. Reform shock-jock Zia Yusuf posted a Zia-bot tweet about the whole thing.
On the topic of Reform and protesters: The leader of the group behind the whole flag-raising thing has been charged with 14 offenses, including racially aggravated harassment, threatening behavior and assault. He was at the Reform conference last week, at their apparent invitation. The Guardian has a writeup.
And on the topic of Reform conference invitees: The original singer of Boney M has condemned her former bandmate who appeared at the Reform conference. PolHome got the scoop.
**Politics is back. As Andy Burnham settles into Downing Street and Westminster returns from recess, Politics at Sam and Anne's cuts through the noise to explain what's really driving the day's biggest political stories. Sam Coates (Sky News) and Anne McElvoy (POLITICO), every weekday by 7.30am. Listen now on your favourite podcast app **
SOCIAL (MEDIA) AFFAIRS
KINDER, GENTLER POLITICS: ITV hack Lewis Denison posted footage of a Reform conference-goer punching him twice while he was being marched out of the main hall after heavies mistook him for a protester.
BEYOND THE M25
ALL ABOARD: Burnham’s best pal Steve Rotheram is the first to benefit from Department for Transport funding to bring buses under public control. The government is giving £90m over the next three years to the Liverpool City Region for the project. ITV has more here.
DEFECTION WATCH: A man called Nigel (but not that one) has become the first councillor to leave Reform UK and join Labour. According to the BBC, Swales said he had “growing concerns about Reform’s ability to deliver at a local level” after being elected to Lancashire County Council 16 months ago. He also cited numerous scandals and a lack of “a serious plan” amongst reasons for quitting.
PAS D’ACCORD: Presidential candidates across the political spectrum are coming out to criticize the immigration memorandum of understanding between Farage and Jordan Bardella. My colleague across the Channel, Victor Foury-Laffont, has a write up of all the backlash — and the one contender staying noticeably quiet.
**A message from Shell UK: Delivering UK growth and competitiveness requires more than investment in infrastructure and energy. It also requires investment in people. That's why Shell works with colleges, training providers, employers and community organisations across the UK to help develop skills and create pathways into jobs. Through our SkillsTransition programme, we're working towards supporting 15,000 people into jobs by 2035. More than 10,000 people have already engaged with this programme. We aim to reach people where barriers to skills development and employment are greatest, supporting stronger communities, a more competitive economy and long-term prosperity. As a UK-headquartered company, Shell is committed to working with partners across the country to equip people with the skills and opportunities needed to contribute to Britain's future success. Find out more, and disclaimer: shell.co.uk/about-us**
TONIGHT’S MEDIA ROUND
LEADING THE NEWS BULLETINS: Channel 5 News (5 p.m.) leads on the anti-immigration protests.
Tom Swarbrick at Drive (LBC, until 6 p.m.): Reform UK councillor Linden Kemkaran.
The News Agents (Podcast, drops at 5 p.m.): Hope not Hate’s Joe Mulhall.
Tonight With Andrew Marr (LBC, 6 p.m.): Tory MP James Cleverly … Labour MP Mike Tapp … Labour MP Dan Tomlinson.
The Cathy Newman Show (Sky News, 7 p.m.): Labour peer Harriet Harman … Tory peer Ed Vaizey … Labour MP Mike Tapp.
The Evening Edition with Kait Borsay (Times Radio, 7 p.m.): Labour MP Jeevun Sandher … former Supreme Court Justice Jonathan Sumption.
Cross Question with Iain Dale (LBC, 8 p.m.): Foreign Affairs Select Committee Chair Emily Thornberry … Tory peer Joanne Cash.
Jacob Rees-Mogg’s State of the Nation (GB News, 8 p.m.): Tory peer John Redwood … Former Labour adviser Scarlett McGwire.
REVIEWING THE PAPERS TONIGHT: Sky News (10 p.m.): Columnist Sarah Vine and the Mirror’s Kevin Maguire … Times Radio (10.30 p.m.): Journo Carolyn Quinn and the FT’s George Parker.
WHERE TO FIND BOOZE IN WESTMINSTER TONIGHT
WASTED WITH WONKS: The Future Governance Forum is holding its autumn reception at One Birdcage Walk from 6 p.m. Invites needed.
DRINK TO FORGET: Political chronicler Anthony Seldon and team launch their tome about the Rishi Sunak administration at Daunt Books in Marylebone from 6.30 p.m.
TOMORROW’S WORLD
WHAT BRITAIN THINKS ABOUT STUFF: The National Centre for Social Research drops its latest update in its social attitudes research.
FULLY COMP: The Competition and Markets Authority has two reports out about public procurement, from 6 a.m.
GETTING THE GANG TOGETHER: Andy Burnham will chair a meeting of his cabinet in the morning.
WHAT THE GOVERNMENT WANTS TO TALK ABOUT: Work experience, space and Ukraine.
IN THE COMMONS: MPs sidle in from 11.30 a.m. for Treasury questions, before the remaining stages of the Health Bill.
IN THE LORDS: New peers Swaran Singh and Nick Stace are sworn in at 2.30 p.m. before questions and the second committee stage debate on the Armed Forces Bill.
BOE SELECTA: Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey appears at the Treasury committee from 2.15 p.m.
ANY OTHER BUSINESS
IN MEMORIAM: Former peer Francis Grosvenor, one of the last two remaining people to have sat in the 1955 parliament, has died at age 92. More detail here.
WHAT I’VE BEEN READING: Lib Dem peer and polling expert Mark Pack goes deeper on his Substack into how the origin of the polls at the center of the Reform foreign donations sting was hidden from Times and Telegraph readers — and alleges that newspapers have done the same in the past with government-funded or other polls. “It’s fair to say that one aspect of the story … is that media outlets have a track record of not being rigorous enough in checking and publishing the full origins of polling data they run,” he writes.
PACKED LUNCH OR PALACE LUNCH: Subject to change, here are the lunch menus on the estate tomorrow: Bellamy’s: Jerk pork with rice and peas; dill hake with fennel seed, pomegranate, parsley, spring onion quinoa and cumin yoghurt; sweet chili tempura tofu with stir-fried vegetables and noodles … The Debate: Cajun chicken with black bean and sweetcorn quinoa, plus avocado; jerk pork with rice and peas; vegetable samosa chaat with chili chutney and tamarind yoghurt … Terrace Cafeteria: Fish finger bap with mushy peas; jerk pork with rice and peas; penne bake with olives, capers and herb crumb … River Restaurant:
ON THIS DAY IN POLITICS: On September 7 2006, Prime Minister Tony Blair confirmed he would step down within 12 months. On the same date in 2019, Work and Pensions Secretary Amber Rudd resigned in protest, after 19 Conservative MPs were stripped of the whip for an anti-Brexit rebellion against the government. On the same date in 2021, Prime Minister Boris Johnson announced a new health and social care tax worth £12 billion to build back from the Covid pandemic and fix the social care crisis. It was later scrapped amid the Conservative leadership wars. On that note, on the same date in 2022, new Prime Minister Liz Truss appointed her cabinet.
WRITING PLAYBOOK TOMORROW MORNING: Andrew McDonald.

summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces a tense grilling from Labour MPs concerned about their seats and communication with leadership. Meanwhile, Chancellor John Healey delivered a speech focused on economic growth, urging ministers to tolerate higher legal risks to speed up decision-making, though the government simultaneously reversed a local council reform policy due to legal advice. Additionally, the by-election date for Keir Starmer's former seat in Holborn and St Pancras has been set for October 8.
key_points: Andy Burnham faces a closed-door meeting with anxious Labour MPs seeking clarity on his leadership priorities and government direction.
Chancellor John Healey pledged to prioritize growth, reform the Treasury's green book, and encouraged ministers to accept higher legal risk to accelerate decisions.
Communities Secretary Angela Rayner announced a U-turn, cancelling and reviewing local council reforms due to legal advice, frustrating backbench MPs.
The by-election for Holborn and St Pancras is scheduled for October 8.
The UK government rejected assertions made by U.S. ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee regarding allegations of 'Jew hate' within the British government.

title: Prince Harry pictured in London as King issues statement on future
author: Matt Watts
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Trump Says He’s Glad Prince Harry And Meghan Markle Left the U.S.](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/07/17/41/Prince-Harry.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
Read More
The Sussexes stepped down as working royals in 2020 but returned to the UK on August 26, with rumours rife as to the reason behind the unexpected development.
The message emphasises that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK - the so-called Sandringham Agreement - is still in place.
In a letter the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior officer of the Royal Household, stated: “Following the decision by the Duke and Duchess of Sussex to relocate to the UK, we have received a number of requests for guidance. To help avoid doubt or confusion, The King has directed that the following information be shared.
“It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of The Sovereign, and are no longer working Members of The Royal Family.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/07/15/64fc9fd7332c8cd6f2cd056a7dcf645dY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg4ODc4OTUx-2.83640582.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“This position, distinct from the State and Royal duties undertaken by the working Royal Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected.”
On Monday a picture emerged of Prince Harry at Tower Bridge Studios, where Diary of a CEO and BBC’s The Apprentice is filmed.
The studio posted two pictures to their Instagram after he signed their wall. The pictures were captioned: “Thank you Prince Harry for choosing Tower Bridge Studios! It was an absolute pleasure to have you in our studios and signing our wall. We look forward to welcoming your back again. “
The news of the family’s return to the UK was therefore met with utter surprise; no official reason has been given, but many have speculated that Harry may want to be back for his father, King Charles, amid the monarch’s ongoing treatment for cancer.
It has been reported that King Charles was only made aware that his youngest child is returning with his family days before the news leaked to the public.
That the Sussexes would relocate to the Cotswolds makes sense, as the area speaks to both Harry’s history and Meghan’s Hollywood connections.
In recent areas, the area, which covers five counties in the south-west of England, has become home to a host of high-profile stars, from the Beckhams to Ellen Degeneres.
Harry also spent much of his childhood around Gloucestershire, Oxfordshire and Wiltshire, including at his father’s private residence, Highgrove, in Tetbury.
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle unexpectedly returned to the UK from the US on August 26, prompting a statement from the King clarifying that the 2020 Sandringham Agreement remains in place. Following the family's return, a letter from the Lord Chamberlain reaffirmed that the couple are no longer working members of the royal family. Meanwhile, Prince Harry was photographed at Tower Bridge Studios after signing their wall, though no official reason for the relocation has been provided.
key_points: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex returned to the UK on August 26 after stepping down as working royals in 2020.
A statement directed by the King confirmed that the 2020 Sandringham Agreement terms remain fully in place.
Prince Harry was recently pictured at Tower Bridge Studios after signing their wall.
No official reason has been given for the return, though King Charles was reportedly notified only days before public leaks.

title: A new sauna is opening at a ‘castle’ in Hackney
author: Caitlin Barr
content:
[title]
You’re far from hard-pressed to find a sauna in east London. There are 48 confirmed sweat-cabins in the region according to SaunaMap's database. Hackney alone boasts three options, including the popular Rooftop Saunas. But there could soon be a fourth place to relax if plans to build a new sauna at the Grade II-listed Stoke Newington Pumping Station are approved.
The site, commonly known as ‘the Castle’ due to its gothic vibes, was built in the 1850s as a solution to London’s growing need for clean water for its rising population, and fell out of use in the late twentieth century. It was rescued from total disrepair in 1995 by being converted into an indoor climbing centre, and it’s now been earmarked by Community Sauna CIC (which runs the nearby Hackney Wick Sauna) to host a new sauna facility suitable for up to 16 people.
According to proposals, there’ll be a dry heated timber sauna structure and two cold showers towards the southern boundary of the climbing centre, but there are no plans for a cold plunge pool at this stage.
Don’t get too excited yet though – there have already been 12 formal objections from residents who claim that noise, glare from LED-lighting, over-development of land set aside for community gardening, and potential crowding of pavements, could all be major issues. The council has stated that adjacent land will not be disturbed, so the gardens will be safe, and that it doesn't predict footfall will rise significantly.
At a planning meeting, Stephen Moorhouse, representing the non-profit, said: ‘Our vision is quite simple: to bring communities together around an activity that improves wellbeing and to make that experience accessible to as many people as possible.’
Town hall planners have recommended that the new sauna site is approved for an initial period of five years, and a final decision is expected in the coming days.
Get the latest and greatest from the Big Smoke – from news and reviews to events and trends. Just follow our Time Out London WhatsApp channel.
Stay in the loop: sign up for our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox.
summary: Plans have been submitted to build a new 16-person sauna at the Grade II-listed Stoke Newington Pumping Station, commonly known as 'the Castle' in Hackney. Proposed by Community Sauna CIC, the facility would feature a dry heated timber structure and two cold showers near the existing indoor climbing centre. While town hall planners have recommended the project for approval, it has drawn 12 formal objections from local residents concerned about noise, lighting, and crowding.
key_points: Community Sauna CIC has proposed a new sauna facility at the Stoke Newington Pumping Station in Hackney.
The proposed sauna would accommodate up to 16 people and include two cold showers.
The project has received 12 formal objections from residents citing concerns over noise, LED glare, and crowding.
Town hall planners have recommended the project be approved for an initial five-year period.

title: Person with 'life-changing' injuries as incident on Tube sparks delays - LIVE
author: Niva Yadav; Matt Watts; Megan Howe
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2024/03/01/08/01080028-af584b8a-aede-4eae-91ee-4c8be31022bf.jpg?crop=8:5,smart&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
A casualty on the tracks at an east London Tube station has led to severe disruption on the London Underground.
Local MP Stella Creasy confirmed the incident on the tracks at Walthamstow Central station this morning, that caused the closure of the entire Victoria line.
It reopened with severe delays that were then downgraded to minor delays mid-afternoon.
The British Transport Police confirmed the incident was not being treated as suspicious and a person had been taken to hospital with “potentially life-threatening injuries”.
Elizabeth line trains will not serve Heathrow Airport Terminal 5 while the Heathrow Express services is running a reduced schedule.
Follow the latest updates below...
Live updates
Moorgate station evacuated due to a fire alert
Moorgate station has been evacuated due to a fire alert.
The station has been closed with three fire trucks outside.
Video shows people waiting outside as the London Fire Brigade attend.
![Moorgate station evacuated due to fire alert](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/fff6f57a-2742-4d68-b6de-f9537bfab546/thumbnail-360.webp)
We’ll provide more details as soon as we get them.
Severe delays continue on the Elizabeth line
Severe delays continue on the Elizabeth line this afternoon between Heathrow Terminals 2&3 and Heathrow Terminal 5.
Engineers are working to fix equipment damaged by vandalism in the Kensal Green area.
Passengers travelling to the airport are advised to use the Piccadilly line to travel to Heathrow Airport and use the free interchange service to travel between terminals.
Elsewhere, there are minor delays between Hayes & Harlington and Reading due to an earlier a vehicle hitting a bridge earlier at Burnham and minor delays between Shenfield and Whitechapel due to an earlier signal system failure at Ilford.
Minor delays on the Metropolitan line
The issue on the Metropolitan line has been cleared, with only minor delays now.
It comes after an earlier signal failure at Amerhsam.
The next southbound train from Amersham will depart at 15:52.
There are also minor delays between Moor Park and Watford while engineers fix a signal failure at Watford.
Delays on Victoria line downgraded to minor
Delays on the Victoria line have been downgraded to minor following a casualty on the tracks earlier this morning.
Casualty rushed to hospital
The person involved in this morning’s incident has been rushed to hospital.
In a statement, the London Ambulance Service confirmed it was called to Walthamstow Central Station to reports of a person on the tracks at around 9:15am.
“We sent resources to the scene including an ambulance crew, an incident response officer, a paramedic in a fast response car and paramedics from our hazardous area response team (HART). We also dispatched London’s Air Ambulance.
“We treated a person at the scene and took them to a major trauma centre by road as a priority,” the statement added.
Metropolitan line part suspended
The Metropolitan line is part suspended between Amersham and Chalfont & Latimer. This is due to a signal failure at Amersham.
There are also minor delays between Watford and Moor Park, but a good service on the rest of the line.
Check before you travel, warns Walthamstow Forest Council
Walthamstow Forest Council is advising Londoners to check before travelling following disruption on the Victoria line on Monday.
As it stands, there are still severe delays on the entire Victoria line following an earlier casualty on the tracks. A person has been rushed to hospital and is believed to be facing “life-changing injuries.”
Bakerloo line part-suspended
The Bakerloo line has been part-suspended between Harrow & Wealdstone and Queen's Park stations due to a faulty train.
Transport for London says there is a good service on the rest of the line.
Severe delays remain on Victoria line
Severe delays remain on the Victoria line this lunchtime after the casualty on the tracks at Walthamstow Central station at shortly after 9am.
Transport for London referring to the casualty as a “earlier customer incident”, said tickets are being accepted on alternate routes.
It said tickets are being accepted on London buses, the Weaver line and the Suffragette line.
Person rushed to hospital with 'life-changing injuries' at Walthamstow Central station
More details on the casualty on the tracks at Walthamstow Central station this morning have been provided by police.
The British Transport Police said they were called to the Victoria line station at 9.15am to reports of a casualty on the tracks.
They said paramedics also attended, and a person was taken to hospital with “potentially life-changing injuries”.
They said the incident was not being treated as suspicious.
![Walthamstow Central Tube station](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/06/30/12/15/Walthamstow_Central.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640)
summary: An incident on the tracks at Walthamstow Central station caused severe disruption and the temporary closure of the entire Victoria line. A person was rushed to a major trauma centre by road with potentially life-changing injuries. British Transport Police confirmed that the incident is not being treated as suspicious. Meanwhile, multiple other London Underground and rail lines also experienced delays and part-suspensions due to signal failures, faulty trains, and vandalism.
key_points: A person was taken to hospital with potentially life-threatening or life-changing injuries following a track incident at Walthamstow Central station.
British Transport Police confirmed the Walthamstow Central incident is not being treated as suspicious.
The Victoria line suffered severe disruption and closures before delays were downgraded later in the day.
Additional transport disruptions affected the Metropolitan, Bakerloo, and Elizabeth lines due to separate issues including signal failures, faulty trains, and equipment damage.

title: Beyond the tourist traps: How top chefs are revamping London's South Bank
author: Josh Barrie
content:
The South Bank renaissance: This time it's for locals
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![The London Question: Should London have a tourist tax?](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/15/Sea-Containers-restaurant.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![The London List](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_going_out_embed_desktop.png)
It’s Saturday on the South Bank and crowds are heaving. The London Eye, almost as old as the first Giraffe World Kitchen restaurant (1998, Hampstead), feels almost old amid all the selfies and Lime bikes. Tourists weave between hot-dog vendors and doughnut stands. Some find respite in the entrance to Sea Life, a once grand aquarium now easily missed along the thoroughfare, and others queue for the London Dungeon, which moved from its more fittingly sinister location in the belly of London Bridge to County Hall in 2013.
The South Bank hasn’t been considered a cool part of town for decades. No district of London with an attraction called Shrek’s Adventure! can possibly inspire reverence or inspire prolonged visits from actual Londoners.
That’s not to say there aren’t cultural touchstones here: the Southbank Centre, the National Theatre, Shakespeare’s Globe, the BFI and Tate Modern are some of London’s best ports of call. They’re world famous, in fact. But it isn’t them, it’s the overall feel of the place — the “vibe” in modern terms — and much of that can be pinned to food and drink. You can enjoy Hockney or Hamlet but you’ll be back over the river to Soho for a drink afterwards, or east to Borough Market for dinner (merhaba, Kismet; bonjour Camille).
Or you would have until recently. These days, increasingly, the South Bank has options. It’s changing, evolving; people are starting to realise that all this brutalism, contemporary art and theatrical stardom is deserving of more than Wagamama, Strada and La Gamba.
These might be fine, to a point — let’s not be snobbish. After all, accessible chains are generally willing and able to cough up for the soaring rents and why wouldn’t they invest in a site with riverside views? But they’re not exciting; they hardly match up to Shakespeare.
![Sea Containers restaurant](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/15/Sea-Containers-restaurant.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
And he’s not opened one of his affordable burger bars or pizza joints. It’s a fully fledged restaurant, serving tagliolini with crab from Brixham, Devon, and his famous beef Wellington. And sure, there are crowd-pleasers.
This isn’t food for Michelin inspectors. His Idiot Sandwich Flight, at £26, attests to that. But it’s a big opening, and it’s a marker in the South Bank sand.
Growing footfall at the South Bank
“Opening a restaurant on London’s South Bank this month feels like the perfect time,” Ramsay tells me while on a flight from the US. “It’s one of the most multicultural and vibrant stretches of the capital — a place where the river brings people together, where street food, cafés and restaurants sit alongside music, theatre and art.”
Ramsay is classically upbeat. Why wouldn’t he be? This is a part of London with a monster footfall; one which, even if Londoners don’t buy into it, will entice an endless deluge of tourists regardless. Last year, South Bank BID, which lobbies for business interests in the area, reported 38 million visitors, representing a 20 per cent growth over two years. But there also seems to be a sense that Londoners are, at least in part, reclaiming this stretch of riverside too. It should be for everyone.
“It’s one of the most multicultural and vibrant stretches of the capital”
Gordon Ramsay
Ramsay adds: “Food here isn’t simply something you eat — it’s part of the culture, the conversation and the energy of the riverside. It’s exciting and that is exactly why we wanted to be here.”
Read More
Ramsay isn’t the only high-profile hospitality man banking on the place. Soon, Jack Croft and Will Murray, of Fallow, one of London’s most lauded restaurants (500,000 Instagram followers and counting), will put their own stamp on the South Bank, albeit in a different guise to Fallow.
Together with business partner James Robson, who’s also led the group to open Roe, in Canary Wharf, and Fowl in Mayfair, they’ve taken on the restaurant space at the Oxo Tower, a landmark that first launched as a hospitality space in 1996. Robson says there’s a “new energy” to the South Bank and taking on the Oxo Tower was ultimately a “no-brainer in 2026”.
![Fallow, soon to be at Oxo Tower](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/48/Fallow-Southbank.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“There’s definitely something happening in the area,” he tells the Standard. “I got the call that the venue was for sale while on holiday, a quick approach, and we owned it 18 days later.
“We moved ultra-fast because it’s an amazing site in an area with enormous potential. The views are incredible.”
Robson says the team won’t be installing a branch of Fallow at the location. Instead, they’ll play to the strengths of the place, separating the 12,500 sq ft site into a chic brasserie on one side and, possibly, a more casual offering on the other. Much is still to be decided, he says. Either way, the current restaurant and bar is to be revamped and updated.
“We’ll be polishing up the offering, giving it more value and a lot more love,” he says. “We’ll lean into the brand too and create something by our chefs. I think there’ll be an elevated concept on one side, and then we’ll draw on the history on the other. We’ve gone in fast, but we always think very carefully.”
Is there money to be made here, beyond the churn of chains and the stream of modest street food vans? “The restaurant is turning over about £10 million a year at the moment.
“Hopefully we’ll double that to get into profit. They’re losing money at the moment. We can turn it around, invest and sharpen the place up; get some economies of scale going. I really think the South Bank is on fire.”
Restaurants are flocking to the area
Robson mentions other restaurant brands soon to arrive. Caravan, a growing group of brunch-style restaurants founded by the Kiwi trio Miles Kirby, Laura Harper-Hinton and Chris Ammermann, is opening at the Southbank Centre, on the terrace, in the old Ping Pong location, in November.
“Borough Market isn’t far away either,” Robson adds. “And there are street food vans everywhere, which is great for passing trade.”
With food and drink comes commerce. It’s little wonder other industries are identifying a blossoming landscape, one that will feed London’s office workers well, as well as affordably and conveniently. Next year, the Lego Group will move its London hub from Farringdon to the South Bank, taking on a 192,000 sq ft space over three and half floors. It shows intent.
Loren I Shuster, chief people officer for Lego, said of the move last May: “We’re excited about moving to the South Bank.
“It’s the cultural heart of London, which makes it the perfect location for a company dedicated to inspiring creativity. 76 Southbank is an iconic building.” Kudos, then, to those with the foresight to have come in early.
“It’s the cultural heart of London”
Loren I Shuster
One is Lasdun, which opened in the National Theatre way back in 2023. If anything, fanfare around the venture wasn’t frenzied enough at the time — judging by today’s standards, anyway, where restaurants are exalted as if Mayan gods — though it did get a four-star review from then Standard critic Jimi Famurewa, and a similarly joyful write-up from Grace Dent. Anyway, Lasdun is the work of Jon Rotheram, Tom Harris and John Ogier, the trio behind the critically acclaimed Hackney pub The Marksman. Today the £32 pre-theatre menu features dishes such as Cornish fish soup, smoked haddock fishcakes and slow-roast Hereford beef with bobby beans and mustard.
Forza had been a part of Peckham’s dining fabric for years, but there came a time to grow. The South Bank was where co-founders and childhood friends Bash Redford and Michael Lavery pitched up (they’ve since opened another restaurant in Soho).
![Forza Wine at the National Theatre](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/39/Forza-Wine-at-the-National-Theatre-PR-shot-CREDIT-Caitlin-Isola.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Redford says: “I don’t want this to sound like a PR soundbite, but I think the South Bank is turning into a place that Londoners want to go. It’s still a place for visitors and tourists, obviously, but ours is a restaurant for locals too. It’s a balancing act. We have to think about everyone.
“For a long time, our nearest competitor was Giraffe. Before we came here, I could count the number of times I’d visited the South Bank on one hand. I suppose it was a prospect, but a gamble too. But we thought, maybe we can make this work.”
Forza Wine can be found on the first floor of the National Theatre. It boasts an enviable terrace overlooking Waterloo Bridge, Embankment and, newly, Nick Jones’ St Clement hotel. Things are happening on both sides of the river.
“We planned it out and we were excited about the footfall,” Redford says. “I do think there’s long been an element of customers playing it safe. Maybe the younger crowd go to known brands and older ones stick to Pizza Express or Brasserie Blanc (Raymond Blanc’s casual chain).
“But we were excited at the time, about the footfall and what we could achieve. I think there’s change happening here and it’s very much a case of ‘the more the merrier’.
“Maybe this part of London was forgotten by the people who live here. There was snobbery around it. Not so much now.”
summary: London's South Bank is undergoing a culinary renaissance, moving away from generic chains and tourist traps to attract top-tier chefs and local diners. High-profile restaurateurs, including Gordon Ramsay, the team behind Fallow, and Caravan, are opening ambitious new venues and revamping landmark spaces in the area. Driven by massive footfall, cultural institutions, and a changing perception of the district, these culinary investments are transforming the South Bank into a vibrant destination for locals.
key_points: Top chefs and prominent restaurant groups, such as Gordon Ramsay and the team behind Fallow, are opening new ventures on the South Bank.
The area, historically dominated by tourist spots and accessible chain restaurants, is increasingly attracting local Londoners.
The South Bank BID reported 38 million visitors last year, representing a 20 percent growth over two years.
Other notable hospitality additions include Caravan at the Southbank Centre, Lasdun at the National Theatre, and Forza Wine.
Major businesses like the Lego Group are also relocating their hubs to the South Bank, signaling broader commercial growth in the area.

title: Drought devastation: How to save London's parched trees
author: Tom Edwards
content:
![Parched yellow grass with a bare tree](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9a5a/live/25293600-a623-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
The summer may be over, but London's trees are still under threat
- Published
In The Closes park in West Drayton, we are surrounded by withered saplings of newly planted trees. It has been a bad summer for the capital's trees - the challenge is significant.
A recent report from the Greater London Authority (GLA) concluded that, if nothing changes, over 72% of London's current public realm tree population, external will struggle under future climatic conditions.
Trees are on the front line in the fight to combat man-made climate change in London.
Trees are meant to make the city more resilient. We need them for shade and protection against extreme heat.
More heatwaves and drought makes planting native trees and maintaining the existing canopy more and more difficult.
The summer may be over, but London's trees are still under threat.
![A young sapling is withered with brown leaves](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/607e/live/793bb110-a622-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
A sapling in West Drayton, Hillingdon
Georgie Power, senior coordinator at Trees for Cities, external (a charity that plants thousands of trees and looks after them) has said this summer had been unlike any other she has experienced.
There has also been a wildfire in the park that has killed many of the saplings.
"Last summer was bad. I think we had three heat waves, kind of back to back, but this summer has been a different level. â©
"It's just been relentless. No rain for over 50 days. Every single site has struggled, and our team has really been put under massive pressure because of that."
She and her team have been trying to water more trees more frequently, and giving them more water when they do it.
"We're giving them from 50 to 60 litres, which might seem small for one tree, but for hundreds of trees, that means much more work.
"We've really worked hard to try and encourage volunteers to come in and help us with the mulching, because that's something that really saves the tree's lives."
![A woman stands in front of a young tree](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/e2cc/live/2e84ccb0-a622-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Georgie Power said this summer's heat had "been a different level"
At Chiswick House and Gardens, external it has also been a tough summer, involving extra watering and mulching.
Rosie Fyles, head of gardens, said many of the trees had started to drop their leaves ahead of autumn in response to the drought and heat.
"It is really reminiscent of autumn - but in fact they're dropping them because they can't support them from a water point of view any more.
"The trees that seem to be having the most difficult time are the trees that we really associate with an English garden or an English landscape.
"Trees will have their lives shortened and over time more trees will die which sounds like a terribly depressing thing to say, but I think there's only so much stress they can withstand."
![A woman waters some plants](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a72d/live/e5ad1710-a6ba-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Chiswick House and Gardens gave their trees extra watering
The aim of the mayor of London is to increase tree canopy cover in London by 10% from 2016 levels.
But trees weakened by heat and drought are often more vulnerable to pests and diseases.
Research is now being done by the Greater London Authority, external into what trees are the best to plant and will be more resilient to climate change. The results should be available next spring.
![A sapling is surrounded by scorched earth](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/3d3a/live/c3e2ac60-a621-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
An increased number of wildfires also pose a threat to trees
CEO of Trees for Cities Kate Sheldon described the summer as "incredibly challenging" for London's trees.
"Imagine standing out here all summer yourself. We've been able to go inside or hide under the shade, and they've been withstanding prolonged heat, prolonged drought for months now. â©So, we're seeing a mixed reaction response in the tree species that we're planting.
"They really need a huge amount of extra help this year, and they will do for future years."
All of that puts pressure on funding and resources at the charity.
![A woman in a green T shirt stands in front of some trees](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/51cd/live/e0115580-a621-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Kate Sheldon, CEO Trees for Cities
How to help trees:
- Watering: Give young trees at least 50 litres of water each week during warmer periods
- Donate a drink: Support our emergency watering efforts,, external to help a thirsty urban tree
- Sponsor a tree: There are ten London boroughs where residents can sponsor a new tree in their neighbourhood, external
- Spread the word: Encourage your friends and family to water trees too or share the message on social media.
Every litre helps. Every tree matters. Every share could inspire someone else to act.
Trees for Cities
![Some withered saplings in a park](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/72d0/live/bca7f9e0-a622-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Many saplings have not survived the summer
The challenge now is working out which trees will survive in a warming London, Sheldon said: "We're working really closely with the Greater London Authority and Kew Gardens who are doing some fantastic groundbreaking research into species selection.
"We can trial different species and also species from different provinces as well that are more used to the hotter and drier effects that we've seen.
"We're going to have hotter drier summers, we're also getting warmer wetter winters.
"The real challenge comes into selecting species that are going to be able to withstand both of those changes, and that's complex."
The charity has also launched a campaign to get Londoners, external to help by watering trees close to them.
![A tree is surrounded by brown leaves](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a1b3/live/475c82a0-a622-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Many trees have dropped their leaves early due to the drought
Workers on the ground are already replacing native species like Alder with Italian Alder which seems to be more resilient to climate change, along with Ginko and European nettle trees.
Georgie Power said she was "very, very, very nervous" about it the future.
"I've studied climate change, and I've been working in the environmental field for a while, but you know what's coming when you study climate change. â©We've known it for decades. But this is really the first summer where I've seen climate change on our doorstep, and it's not going anywhere."
"This is the new norm, this is going to happen again next year. â©So we have to figure out what our infrastructure's going to be like, how do we engage with the public?
"What do the public need to do in their own private gardens as well and in our community spaces with the trees we've planted?â©
"The only option we have is to adjust for the future."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: London's trees and newly planted saplings faced severe stress this summer due to relentless heatwaves, prolonged drought, and wildfires. A Greater London Authority report warns that over 72% of the city's public realm trees will struggle under future climatic conditions if nothing changes. Charities and garden teams are responding by increasing watering frequency, using mulch, and researching climate-resilient tree species.
key_points: Over 72% of London's public realm trees could struggle under future climatic conditions according to a GLA report.
The summer drought, lack of rain for over 50 days, and wildfires have killed many newly planted saplings.
Organizations like Trees for Cities and Chiswick House are providing extra watering and mulching to save stressed trees.
The Greater London Authority and Kew Gardens are researching more climate-resilient tree species to plant in the future.

title: More night buses and police needed to boost capitalâs nightlife, according to Westminster Council | LBC
author: Isobel Anderson Morris
content:
More night buses and police needed to boost capitalâs nightlife, according to Westminster Council
Westminster Council said it had consulted residents, businesses and visitors as it prepared proposals to improve Londonâs nighttime economy.
A greater number of night buses, a more visible police presence and a 24-hour Tube service on Thursdays would help support and boost Londonâs nightlife, according to Westminster Council.
Listen to this article
Pouring more funding into late-night transport, including by funding improvements to taxi and private hire options, would limit closing-time crowds and help people leave the area with greater safety, it said.
Westminster Council said it has heard from residents, the capitalâs businesses and visitors, who have called for a greater police presence on Londonâs streets to help people feel safe on a night out, which would also help the hospitality industry.
The urging for increased resources comes after a dispute regarding Westminsterâs draft licensing policy, which was criticised for proposing to reduce standing-up drinking in Sohoâs pubs, dubbed âvertical drinkingâ.
Those responding to a consultation on draft changes to Westminsterâs licensing policy âconsistently askedâ for greater support for licensed venues including bars, pubs and nightclubs, the council reported.
Talking about the proposed changes, Westminsterâs deputy leader Tim Barnes said: âA lack of investment in policing has left the Met objecting to many licensing applications over public safety concerns.
Read more: Women and girls to shape Â£15.6m plan to make London safer
Read more: Uber and AI firm Wayve launch first self-driving robotaxis in London
âPeople struggle to get home from a night out when late-night bus routes have been cut and overnight Tube services are non-existent during the week.
âWeâve spent the summer taking feedback from residents, the hospitality industry and visitors.
âWeâll take this on board and do our bit to support the hospitality industry, but we need the mayorâs team to fund the services which make London a 24-hour city.â
Regarding the consultation on draft changes to Westminsterâs licensing policy, a council spokesman has now confirmed there will not be a blanket ban on new licensed venues in Soho, and the policy wording will be updated to make this clear.
Westminster oversees more than 4,000 pubs, nightclubs, restaurants and bars, including those in Soho, Leicester Square, Piccadilly Circus and Covent Garden.
A spokeswoman for Lord Sadiq Khan said he is âcommitted to doing everything he can to make Londonâs high streets thriveâ, pointing to falling rates of knife enabled crime and theft in the capital.
She added that the amount of police officers in the West End has doubled, and the number of phone thefts have dropped by 50% in the area.
The spokeswoman said: âIn addition, Sadiqâs newly opened Command Cell in the heart of the West End is now serving as a central point for police and partners to share intelligence, identify suspects and co-ordinate action to make our streets safer for Londoners and visitors alike.
âThe mayor is also helping people travel safely and affordably at all hours with Londonâs Night Tube.
âIt provides a vital boost for our night-time economy, supporting local businesses across the capital and keeping London moving around the clock.â
summary: Westminster Council has called for increased night buses, a more visible police presence, and 24-hour Thursday Tube services to support London's nighttime economy and improve safety. Following consultations with residents, businesses, and visitors, the council urged the mayor's team to fund these essential late-night transport and security services. Additionally, the council confirmed there will be no blanket ban on new licensed venues in Soho under its updated licensing policy.
key_points: Westminster Council proposes more night buses, increased police visibility, and Thursday 24-hour Tube services to boost London's nightlife.
Consultations revealed that stakeholders want greater support for licensed venues and improved safety when leaving late-night areas.
The council has clarified that its updated licensing policy will not impose a blanket ban on new licensed venues in Soho.
The mayor's office responded by highlighting existing measures, including doubled police officers in the West End, the Night Tube, and a new Command Cell.

title: Growth cannot be reserved for London warns Chancellor ahead of major speech
author: Rachael Burford
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
He is pressing ahead with major reforms to the Treasury “rule book” to drive investment out of the capital to the regions and is changing the discount rate on which the value of transport, housing and social infrastructure projects is assessed.
“But not growth for its own sake – not a number on a spreadsheet. And not reserved for our biggest cities. This is about growth in every postcode,” he wrote.
“Factories across Britain taking on young people. Small business owners finally being able to expand. Town centres and high streets seeing new life.”
![Higher UK borrowing costs could threaten Chancellor John Healey’s fiscal headroom at the Budget (Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/02/12/298f91173a580e90b4dfc367c81a4f22Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg4NDM2MDcz-2.85459686.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Mr Healey added: “Britain already has the strengths it needs to succeed – global financial centres, cutting-edge science and technology, world-class universities, and communities full of ambition. So the question is: What’s stopping us?
“Tomorrow I’ll set out my plan to deliver good growth in every postcode by making the most of Britain’s strengths.
“We’re putting mayors, local government, entrepreneurs and investors at the heart of this plan.”
He warned this could be tough, as US President Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East affects the UK economy.
Economists have predicted that the fiscal buffer Rachel Reeves built up in her last budget, through a combination of tax rises and departmental spending cuts, will be squeezed by the inflationary pressures of ongoing global turmoil.
Read More
Londoners are set to bear the brunt of a number of tax rises in the coming months.
The Labour government has slashed central funding for Wandsworth, Westminster, Hammersmith and Fulham, the City of London and Kensington and Chelsea council, effectively forcing them to significantly raise their low council tax levels next year or drastically cut services.
The Chancellor told the FT: “What’s happening in the Middle East is hitting inflation, it’s hitting growth, it’s hitting borrowing costs.”
He added: “It’s part of a more dangerous world that is more uncertain and it’s one of the challenges we have to meet in this country, but have to meet with other (countries).”
Former Tory PM and Chancellor Rishi Sunak warned Mr Healey must cut spending in his first Budget next month rather than hiking taxes.
He argued that the move should be signalled in advance to calm shaky money markets.
Mr Sunak wrote in The Sunday Times: “He should make clear that he’ll not increase taxes in the budget and that if adjustments need to be made, he’ll cut spending.
“That would provide the certainty needed in an increasingly uncertain world.”
summary: Chancellor John Healey is advancing major Treasury reforms to drive economic growth out of London and into the regions ahead of his upcoming budget. He warned that global challenges, including the conflict in the Middle East, are impacting inflation, growth, and borrowing costs, creating a difficult fiscal environment. Meanwhile, London councils face reduced central funding that will likely force significant tax increases or service cuts, while former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak advises the Chancellor to cut spending rather than raise taxes.
key_points: The Chancellor is reforming the Treasury rule book and discount rates to shift investment to regional transport, housing, and infrastructure projects.
Global economic pressures, including conflict in the Middle East, are negatively impacting UK inflation, growth, and borrowing costs.
Central funding cuts to several London councils are expected to force significant council tax increases or drastic service reductions.
Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak has warned the Chancellor to signal spending cuts rather than tax hikes in the upcoming budget to calm money markets.

title: Diana memorial fountain shut all summer by technical fault
author: James W Kelly
content:
![A wide, curving granite water channel of the Diana Memorial Fountain sitting empty and dry in Hyde Park, with dry leaves scattered in the basin and trees in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/8a4c/live/1db64540-a7c0-11f1-b5cf-8556ae508a51.jpg)
The Diana Memorial Fountain has been closed since at least the start of July
- Published
The Diana Memorial Fountain in Hyde Park - which has long been a popular place to cool down in hot weather - has been kept dry all summer due to a technical fault.
Royal Parks, the charity that maintains the central London park, apologised to visitors who found it without water "particularly given the prolonged high temperatures we've been experiencing".
The fountain opened in 2004 in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales who died nearly seven years earlier.
The closure was initially triggered by a mechanical breakdown in the pump that draws water from the local borehole. The pump was fixed, but software used to control the system then failed, preventing the water supply from being restored.
The closure was publicly announced by Royal Parks on 1 July.
The charity's spokesperson acknowledged that the fountain had "remained dry for longer than we hoped" while specialist teams worked to resolve the software issue.
![A large crowd of adults and children paddling and splashing in the shallow water of the Diana Memorial Fountain on a sunny day, with grassy parkland in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/0c77/live/606c8480-a7c0-11f1-b5cf-8556ae508a51.jpg)
The fountain has long been a popular place to paddle and cool down
The same water supply network feeds several other locations across the capital's Royal Parks, compounding broader operational pressures faced by maintenance staff over the summer.
The memorial undergoes regular year-round maintenance and investment, with officials expecting water to begin flowing again "in the next few weeks".
![A sign and a wooden bin display notices reading "Temporary Downtime: Due to a system issue the fountain is currently dry" beside dry grass and the empty memorial track.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/8c96/live/958273f0-a7c0-11f1-b5cf-8556ae508a51.jpg)
Provisional Met Office figures suggest summer 2026 was the hottest on record
It is not the first time the Â£3.6m memorial fountain, which was officially opened by the late Queen Elizabeth in July 2004, has had to shut down.
Just weeks after it opened, it closed temporarily after three visitors slipped and hurt themselves while paddling.
In January 2005, the memorial closed for four months' renovation work, primarily to tackle problems of flooding and waterlogged ground around the site.
The following summer, ministers blamed members of the public who littered and caused drains to block. This caused a 10 day closure.
Additional reporting by Ewan Somerville.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: The Diana Memorial Fountain in Hyde Park remained closed and dry throughout the summer due to a technical fault. Initially triggered by a mechanical breakdown in the water pump, the closure was prolonged by a subsequent software failure. Royal Parks apologized for the disruption during prolonged high temperatures and expects water to flow again within the next few weeks.
key_points: The Diana Memorial Fountain was shut all summer due to a technical fault.
A mechanical breakdown in the pump and a subsequent software failure prevented the water supply from being restored.
Royal Parks apologized to visitors affected by the dry fountain during high temperatures.
The same water supply network also feeds several other locations across London's Royal Parks.
Officials expect water to begin flowing again in the next few weeks.

title: London basks in autumn sun as capital nears 28C in warm spell
author: Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/10/18/01KZP79WH85Z639KVV716FK1A8.jpg?trim=70,0,70,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Much of the rest of England and Wales has also seen temperatures in the mid-20s, while parts of central and southern Europe have been baked in intense heat, with some spots exceeding 45C.
On Thursday, Huelva in Spain reached a staggering 45.7C, as the country experienced its hottest day of 2026.
The warmth in the capital, however, will be short-lived according to upcoming forecasts.
Temperatures for the forthcoming week suggest highs in the low 20s, with the possibility of showers.
Tuesday seems set to be breezy with sunny spells, followed by a windy Wednesday and a dry Thursday, with light winds and hazy sunshine.
Longer term, the national forecaster suggests that London should expect some longer dry spells as we head toward mid-September.
Temperatures will probably be close to average overall, though still with some relatively cool nights at times.
summary: London and much of England and Wales have experienced a warm autumn spell with temperatures nearing 28C, contrasting with intense heat exceeding 45C in parts of southern and central Europe. However, this warm weather in the capital will be short-lived, with upcoming forecasts predicting highs in the low 20s and potential showers next week. Longer-term forecasts indicate London can expect longer dry spells toward mid-September with temperatures close to average.
key_points: London and parts of England and Wales saw warm temperatures nearing 28C and the mid-20s.
Huelva in Spain reached a staggering 45.7C on Thursday, marking the country's hottest day of 2026.
Forecasts for the upcoming week in London predict lower highs in the low 20s and possible showers.
The national forecaster expects longer dry spells for London heading toward mid-September with near-average temperatures.

title: For the first time in 350 years, this historic London landmark could be getting a visitor centre
author: Katie Forge
content:
![A side by side image of the monument in the city of London](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/04104518/Copy-of-FACEBOOK-SPLIT-IMAGE-59-1024x576.png) 
Whilst London certainly isn’t thin on the ground when it comes to its legendary landmarks, only one of the city’s many monuments is the Monument. Built to honour one of the most significant events in British history, this tall stone column was created as a commemoration of the Great Fire of London – and has been proudly overlooking the Square Mile for 350 years now.
Perched just 62 metres away from Pudding Lane (the very spot in which the Great Fire broke out in 1666), the Monument was designed by iconic architect, Christopher Wren, alongside scientist, Dr Robert Hooke. Built from Portland stone across a six-year period, the Monument officially opened to the public in 1677 as a celebration of the city’s resurgence – and now stands as a much-loved legacy of Old London.
Approximately 200,000 people ascend the structure’s spiral staircase each year to feast their eyes on one of the very best views in London. But that number could soon reach new heights, because – for the first time in 350 years – the Monument could be getting an actual visitor centre.
![The monument commemorating the Great Fire of London](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/04110113/The_Monument_-_geograph.org_.uk_-_3087765-1024x714.jpg)
The Monument currently only boasts a small entrance and ticket desk, but the demolition of the structure’s next door neighbour could pave the way for a ground-floor visitor centre. The building in question is Faryners House, a Brutalist-style structure that was named after the baker who may (or may not) have started the Great Fire of London. The demolition of this building would make room for a new office – but the redevelopment plans could also feature a dedicate visitor space.
The proposed plans come courtesy of the architectural aficionados over at Fletcher Priest Architects. Inside the prospective visitor centre, there would be be an exhibition about the Great Fire of London and a cafe. Plans are still very much in the early stages, but if they are approved, construction could start next year. And the Monument could be welcoming its shiny new visitor centre shortly after.
summary: The historic Monument in London, which commemorates the Great Fire of London, may receive its first-ever visitor centre after 350 years. Proposed by Fletcher Priest Architects, the new space would feature a cafe and an exhibition about the Great Fire. The project is made possible by the planned demolition of the neighbouring Faryners House.
key_points: The Monument was designed by Christopher Wren and Dr Robert Hooke to commemorate the Great Fire of London.
Approximately 200,000 people visit the structure annually.
The proposed visitor centre depends on the demolition of the neighbouring Faryners House.
Plans for the centre include an exhibition about the Great Fire and a cafe.
